analysis: Examined ClusterServiceControl.swift base/head and the test registration in ClusterConsoleCheck.swift. There are three changes. (1) ensureControlResponder (head 109-119) replaces cableMove/controlCableCheck with listenerChange/controlCheck. The control responder is now also torn down and rebuilt when the pairing changes. The listener now uses listenerSelection() and listening.controlPort/listening.policy instead of context.linkSelection() and the fixed ClusterSetupLinkExchange.controlPort. (2) ensureControl (head 176-182) drops the cached ClusterControlNode when node.localID differs from pairing.localMemberID, i.e. a local re-key. This tightens stale-state handling: an old-pairing control node can no longer survive a re-pair with a new local key. (3) The test adds a listenersFollowThePairing group (head 64). The lease handler still binds to the pairing captured at responder creation. Rebuilding on pairing change narrows the window in which an old-pairing key could be answered, so this looks like a hardening. No changed line weakens lease acceptance: receiveLease and its gating are unchanged. The coordinator WebSocket, attestation, App Attest authorization, encryption, prefix cache and add-on hold paths are not touched. Assets and threats A-001, A-016, TB-011, T-041 and TB-012 are unaffected by this local cluster-control listener change. The distributed cluster pairing link is not modeled in the canonical threat model, so this is not a new attack surface relative to it. Unverified contracts outside the supplied source, for integration: listenerChange, controlCheck, listenerSelection(), listening.policy and listening.controlPort are not visible. Integration should confirm three things. First, listening.policy does not widen the bind address or interface beyond the pairing-selected link. Second, a non-fixed controlPort cannot be chosen by an unpaired peer. Third, the Responder still enforces pairing-keyed authentication (S07) for all policies. sendLease still uses context.linkSelection() (head 275) while the responder uses listenerSelection(), which is an asymmetry worth confirming as intended. None of this is evidence of a regression.
